verdict.tagline: Vast worlds and voiced quests stumble over heavy launchers and dated tech.
for_you_if: you want massive story-driven worlds to explore solo
you enjoy deep crafting systems and detailed player housing
not_for_you_if: you are short on storage space for massive downloads
you will not install a separate external launcher
you want a traditional character power progression curve

claims.claim: Reviewers experience frequent crashes on startup and during the opening phase, accompanied by error-handling loops in the launcher that repeatedly prompt file repairs.

citations.review_text: I played this to the end on the EA server years ago and had no problem. I tried the game on Steam and it remembered me from before at a level of 42. That's great, but now it crashes every 5 minutes. Trying to load the game at the start sent me through many hoops of accepting various pages of details. That was already borderline rage-quiting threatening. But the crashing is just too much. The Steam transfer failed terribly. It is unplayeable, 10/100

IM really mad i bought this... AGAIN1! on two seperate computers on two seperate internet connections i've downloaded this game. every time it runs for 2-3 minutes then crashes. I uninstalled and reinstalled on both consoles and have the same problem. I always loved skyrim and wanted to love this, but it doesn't seem like it was meant to be.

0/10 First Impression. Absolutely Unacceptable.

Forty-three minutes. That's how long I spent trying to play a game I had already paid for.

The experience went like this: install, launch, crash, repair files, launch again, crash, repair again, finally reach the title screen, get sent to create an online account and accept legal agreements, return to the game... and it crashes again. Then the launcher tells me to repair the files yet again.

I repaired the installation multiple times. It made absolutely no difference.

The only part of this entire process that worked flawlessly was taking my money. After that I was immediately pushed toward creating another account, accepting additional agreements, being introduced to a subscription service, and exposed to in-game microtransactions before I could even play. Meanwhile, the actual game couldn't stay running long enough to let me create a character.

This is one of the worst first impressions I've had in years. A game should work before it starts asking me for subscriptions and additional purchases.

If your launcher's solution to every crash is "repair the game files," even after repeated successful repairs, then your launcher isn't diagnosing the problem—it's wasting the player's time.

I wanted to enjoy this game. Instead, I spent nearly an hour troubleshooting software I had just installed. That's not entertainment; it's unpaid technical support.

Fix your launcher. Fix your crash handling. Let people actually play the game they purchased before trying to sell them anything else.

citations.review_text:
WARNING! BUYING THE GOLD ROAD COLLECTION WON'T GIVE YOU ACCESS TO ALL OF THE GAME'S CONTENT!

EDIT: THE NEW PREMIUM EDITION DOESN'T CONTAIN ALL OF THE GAME'S CONTENT EITHER!

Elder Scrolls Online's ACTUAL cost far exceeds what the Store Page would lead you to believe. The latest Collection/Edition "only" gives you access to the new major Zones and their Storylines, which granted is a good chunk of the game's content, BUT, what the Store Page DOESN'T tell you, is that the game also has a ton of DLCs within the in-game Crown Store that contain additional content NOT INCLUDED in the latest Expansion pack, and this DLC content includes substantial things like Zones, additional Questlines and even Dungeons. It's not just cosmetic stuff, but actual content you'd want.

In order to get access to all of the game's content you need to buy the latest Expansion pack AND all the additional DLCs within the in-game store using their fake currency, OR, buy the latest Expansion pack AND an ESO+ Subscription, which also gives you access to all the DLCs, but only for as long as you maintain the Subscription.

If you wanted to OWN all the content this game has to offer, you'd need to spend well over 100$, even at a discount.

The ACTUAL cost of the game is intentionally obscured by deceptive marketing and vague language that's "technically" legal, but definitely unethical

The Review

I really wanted to love ESO because the Elder Scrolls universe is great, but the monetization makes it incredibly hard for me to enjoy.

You already buy the game and expansions, and then there's an optional subscription on top of that if you want the experience to feel more convenient. Then you have the Crown Store, cosmetics, DLC, loot-style items and all the other things being sold separately.

I understand that MMOs need a steady source of income, but ESO sometimes feels like it's designed to constantly remind you that there's another thing you could pay for.

The game itself has a lot of content and the world is fun to explore, but the whole business model just takes away from it for me. I don't want to feel like I'm managing a subscription and a virtual wallet while I'm trying to enjoy an RPG.

3/10 — I wanted to explore Tamriel, not explore the Crown Store.

claims.claim: The game features fully voice-acted dialogue for quests and characters.

citations.review_text:
The Elder Scrolls Online (ESO) is the absolute gold standard for modern MMORPGs. It seamlessly blends the massive scale of an online multiplayer world with the deep, narrative-driven freedom of a classic single-player Elder Scrolls game. After hundreds of hours in Tamriel, I can confidently say this is the best MMO on the market.

[b]PROS:[/b]

*   [b]Massive & Varied PvP Modes:[/b] Whether you want large-scale faction warfare or tight team skirmishes, the PvP is incredible. You can join the Alliance War in Cyrodiil to siege massive castles with hundreds of players and siege engines, control the Imperial City in high-stakes PvPvE, or jump into fast-paced 4v4v4 Battlegrounds for quick combat fixes.
*   [b]Complete Play-Your-Way Freedom:[/b] Thanks to the "One Tamriel" system, the entire world scales to your level. You can travel to any zone (like Skyrim, Morrowind, or Elsweyr) right from level one and play with friends regardless of level gaps.
*   [b]Fully Voiced Storytelling:[/b] Every single line of dialogue in the game is fully voice-acted. Quests feel like genuine Elder Scrolls stories rather than tedious, text-heavy fetch chores.
*   [b]Dynamic Action Combat:[/b] No rigid, tab-target cooldown rotations here. Combat relies on active dodging, blocking, weapon swapping, and real-time skill execution, giving it a very high skill ceiling.
*   [b]Limitless Build Flexibility:[/b] Any class can use any weapon, wear any armor type, and fulfill any role (Tank, Healer, or DPS). You have total freedom to craft your ideal playstyle.
*   [b]No Gear Treadmill:[/b] ESO respects your time. Once you hit the Champion Point gear cap, your armor sets stay relevant. You can take a break from the game for months and return without your hard-earned gear being instantly obsolete.

[b]CONS:[/b]

*   [b]Inventory Management without ESO Plus:[/b] Managing your inventory can become tedious without the unlimited crafting bag provided by the optional ESO Plus subscription.

[b…
Mediocre alone unless you're a lore junkie and can enjoy the dialogue. Which is nice. It's fully voiced. But kind of a better and more fleshed out experience with friends.

cohorts.summary: Mid-tier players enjoy solo-friendly progression and vast detailed zones despite stiff combat animations and flat leveling power.

claims.claim: The game features a leveling and progression system where damage does not meaningfully increase at higher levels, giving players tools rather than a power increase.

citations.review_text:
I've put in 30 hours and I'm bored, but I want to be fair about this.

The world is massive and genuinely beautiful. Every zone has a distinct identity, the lore is deep and consistently written, and if you're a lore nerd this is a goldmine.
Every quest is voiced, every NPC has a name, every zone has a history. It feels like a living world in a way most MMOs never achieve.

It's also extremely solo-friendly and casual-friendly. There's very little FOMO.
You can log in for 30 minutes, log in for 6 hours, take a month off – you're never really "behind."
No raid lockouts, no weekly resets that punish you. That's a breath of fresh air not gonna lie.

The fashion build options are absurd. You can make your character look however you want, mix and match. It's a whole layer of self-expression that most MMOs treat as an afterthought at best.

The progression system is, and I don't say this lightly, incomprehensibly dull. You level up to 50 and your damage doesn't meaningfully change. Your HP might even go down once the level-scaling boost falls off. A level 1 character with a level 1 sword deals roughly the same damage as a level 50 character with a max-level sword.

The "power fantasy" that should be the backbone of any RPG (to an extent) is completely absent. You grind, you level up and... nothing happens. You just get more tools, not more power.

The Champion Point system (the post-level-50 "progression") is equally baffling.
You're supposed to feel like you're growing, but you're really just unlocking more slots to swap between builds that all do roughly the same damage. It's horizontal progression disguised as vertical progression.

Battlefield PvP was pretty dead, the matchmaking took forever.

And while the base game is a one-time purchase (which I respect), the ESO Plus subscription gives you material bags that make crafting significantly easier and cheaper. It's not hard pay-to-win, but it's not nothing either. If you don't want to pay the subsc…

[h2]An Absolute Masterpiece[/h2]
Even though I feel like I’ve barely scratched the surface of what Tamriel has to offer, ESO has already completely hooked me. It’s vast, immersive, and full of character. Here is a breakdown of what makes it shine — and where it stumbles.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3790685163
[h2]Fashion & Customization[/h2]
If you love character customization, [b]you are in paradise.[/b]

[list]
[*] [b]Earnable Fashion:[/b] Almost all cosmetics can be obtained completely for free just by playing the game.

[*] [b]Aesthetically Pleasing:[/b] Unlike WoW, where players often run around looking like blinding, eye-searing neon explosions, ESO’s cosmetics are generally much more grounded.

[*] [b]For the Flashy Ones:[/b] Don't worry, if you do want to shine like a walking neon Christmas tree, the option is there. It just takes a bit of time to put your ultimate outfit together.
[/list]

[h2]Immersive Quests[/h2]
The storytelling pulls you in right from the very first second. Because of the incredible immersion, you often forget you're playing an MMO at all. While WoW often tells you to go [b]kill 10 boars and collect 5 pelts,[/b] ESO’s quests are infinitely more sophisticated.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3802948056
[h2]The Biggest Flaw[/h2]
A veteran player with tens of thousands of hours under their belt will kill a mob in roughly the same time as you, a fresh Level 1 newbie.

Being a newcomer who just stepped into the game, you can safely walk through the entire world and never die to random enemies. But for me, this is actually very sad, because it completely kills the sense of difficulty and the genuine fear of powerful monsters.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the combat animations as stiff or janky, and state that the combat mechanics can feel repetitive or spammy.

citations.review_text: Been many years since I tried ESO out and while some things have changed for the better, the gameplay remain as boring as it was from the launch. The same few spells/skills and while there are many "skill lines", you are prevented from playing around with it, creating more interesting combos. So its rinse and repeat attacks over and over and over. And while the "map" is huge, the lack of variation in gameplay just makes it another background. The way quests work seems designed to be confusing - so many quests, so many places - the freedom is good, but the result is an overflow of quests taken here and there until you have no idea where og why you are running to and fro - all the while pressing the same few skill buttons over and over again. No wonder, they can't get people to pay-to-play now-a-days.

i have tried to give this game a shot multiple times
the atmosphere, art and sounds are immersive and its one of the things that i stuck around for the time i did. I couldn't see much value otherwise for the rest - and as great as art and atmosphere is i must say it has failed to deliver an engaging experience to me for the following reasons. 

this is a very dated formula. i personally believe this is targeted for a nostalgic millennial audience who are playing this with rose tinted glasses of a time long gone - there is so much glup-shitto in terms of narrative. 
We are introduced to several random characters with a bunch of random places and names mentioned with very little context, even for fetch quests there is a whole lore dump for no good reason or again - missing context. world building is one thing, but the writing is so uninteresting that i don't even care about what or who is mentioned or enough to find out about them. 

the gameplay is so dated, there's nothing hooking me to even see past the slop narrative. Combat feels spammy animations aren't fluid and feel janky and stiff - i don't mind repetition and i have played MMO's like destiny or Korean MMOs like lost ark etc. which have a lot more engaging, smooth  modern gameplay for MMORPG standards to stick around even for the badly delivered narrative,  so at least there is a redeeming factor there. I have also seen comments like " hurr durr it gets better after 100 hours give it time" - i do not understand such logic... its like telling someone the meal they ordered at a restaurant tastes like shit for the first few bites but they should keep eating it cause it tastes a lot better towards the end guys!!! 

I hear often that MMO's are a dying genre and that there's not enough being made anymore but honestly i think  most of the active modern  player base with available free time does not want to play a game that's catered to nostalgic boomers who are okay with such substandard dated and janky mechanics

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game offers a solo-friendly experience with minimal fear of missing out and no rigid raid lockouts.

citations.review_text:
I've put in 30 hours and I'm bored, but I want to be fair about this.

The world is massive and genuinely beautiful. Every zone has a distinct identity, the lore is deep and consistently written, and if you're a lore nerd this is a goldmine.
Every quest is voiced, every NPC has a name, every zone has a history. It feels like a living world in a way most MMOs never achieve.

It's also extremely solo-friendly and casual-friendly. There's very little FOMO.
You can log in for 30 minutes, log in for 6 hours, take a month off – you're never really "behind."
No raid lockouts, no weekly resets that punish you. That's a breath of fresh air not gonna lie.

The fashion build options are absurd. You can make your character look however you want, mix and match. It's a whole layer of self-expression that most MMOs treat as an afterthought at best.

The progression system is, and I don't say this lightly, incomprehensibly dull. You level up to 50 and your damage doesn't meaningfully change. Your HP might even go down once the level-scaling boost falls off. A level 1 character with a level 1 sword deals roughly the same damage as a level 50 character with a max-level sword.

The "power fantasy" that should be the backbone of any RPG (to an extent) is completely absent. You grind, you level up and... nothing happens. You just get more tools, not more power.

The Champion Point system (the post-level-50 "progression") is equally baffling.
You're supposed to feel like you're growing, but you're really just unlocking more slots to swap between builds that all do roughly the same damage. It's horizontal progression disguised as vertical progression.

Battlefield PvP was pretty dead, the matchmaking took forever.

And while the base game is a one-time purchase (which I respect), the ESO Plus subscription gives you material bags that make crafting significantly easier and cheaper. It's not hard pay-to-win, but it's not nothing either. If you don't want to pay the subsc…

This game is, hands down, the best way to experience the world and lore of the Elder Scrolls.  There is just so much to do and see, seven classes and a huge amount of skills, crafting, resource gathering, trading, and of course combat and quests.  It is also probably the most solo friendly MMO I have played.  The graphics and music are also right up there, maybe the best of this generation of MMOs, not sure as I haven't played all the MMOs out there lol

One thing to note, by paraphrasing masters from both sides of the force, "The FOMO is strong in this one."  Though to be fair this is a hallmark of ALL MMOs!

Highly recommended.

citations.review_text: Love this game! been playing for years , one of the best MMOs out there , the community is nice and helpful , new zones and events around the year so much stuff to do . very free to play friendly you can get most of the shop cosmetics for free by doing tasks ingame and earning currency and they are adding DLCs to base game little by little so you dont have to buy these any more , the only down side is the eso plus sub to unlock the crafting bag

What 4,088 hours in Tamriel teaches you:
After more than four thousand hours, you stop playing ESO just for the loot and start playing it for the world. Few MMOs respect your time and let you play at your own pace quite like this one.
The Good:
• Unmatched World & Lore: Exploring every corner of Tamriel never gets old, and the sheer volume of voiced quests makes the world feel alive.
• Play Your Way: Whether you want to be a hardcore trial raider, a Cyrodiil PvP regular, a master crafter, or spend six months decorating a single house, the endgame is whatever you make it.
• Horizontal Progression: Taking a break doesn't make your gear obsolete. You can step away and come right back without feeling left behind.
The Bad:
• Monetization & Inventory: Playing without ESO Plus for the Craft Bag is a test of patience, and the Crown Store can feel aggressive at times.
• Combat & Balance: Light-attack weaving takes getting used to, and constant class balance changes can be exhausting for long-time players.
Verdict: It isn't a flawless game, and after 4,088 hours I know every quirk and bug by heart—but no other MMO has earned this much of my time. Highly recommended.

I recommend this game even for f2p but if you want to get into Crafting and such you will might find inventory for crafting material to be very hard to maintain and may pay up for the subscription fee otherwise for the game content the game offers a lot for free to play.
Game is fully voice over and although the graphics has aged it still looks pretty darn good in today in full max settings

Knowledge in this game is stronger than everything else.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that new characters are dropped into the middle of the game world without clear guidance on how to start the original quests.

citations.review_text:
This game will always have a special place in my heart. I played since the Beta and loved the promise it showed after release. However, after playing FFXIV, it's clear the respect for current subscribers isn't there. This game feels like it's money farming using nostalgia for other Elder Scrolls games.

- Mounts and outfits that are reskins/re-colorings of previously released items.
- The lack of character customizations (and the ugliness of the characters in general)
- The new character experience is so muddled. It makes the story and lore feel highly optional. 
- The moderation is not great. I once saw a player-ran slave auction take place.

Man, I really wanted to get back into this game after like 4 years off. They just added way too much garbage into it. There's so much monetized bloat that it feels dirty to play. Not only that, they throw new characters into the middle of the game and don't tell you how to get back to the beginning. I had to find a guide online to show me how to start the game normally.

There's constant blinking icons everywhere trying to get you to spend money. It's constant and hard to ignore. I'm telling you right now, the new player experience is gross compared to what it was years ago. Immediately feeling lost isn't great.
